newsitem.title: Australia: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: BRITISH DOCTOR ALLOWED TO STAY IN AUST

Royal Brisbane Hospital radiologist, Duncan Walker, says he has no bitterness towards Australian authorities, despite it taking two-years and a public campaign to allow him and his family to stay in Australia.
Immigration Minister, Philip Ruddock, has reversed a ruling that the Walkers must return to England because their Australian-born daughter, Rosie, has Cerebral Palsy.
Dr Walker says when he got the phone call from the Minister's office, his initial reaction was disbelief.
"We feel very encouraged by the amount of support that we have had since our case became more widely known," Dr Walker said.
He said the support the family had received in Australia, including that from his colleagues and friends at the hospital, had been very moving.
WARNING ABOUT RESPIRATORY DISEASE AMONG CHILDREN
Parents with children under two have been warned to be on the look out for a potentially fatal respiratory disease.
The New South Wales Health department says more than 170 cases of bronchiolitis have been reported since the start of winter.
The department's Dr Jeremy McAnulty says very young babies and those with heart and lung conditions are most at risk.
Symptoms include a fever, wheezy chest, runny nose, coughing and loss of appetite.
Dr McAnulty says bronchiolitis, which is highly infectious, can prove fatal if the symptoms are neglected.
ABORIGINES CLAIM CONTINUOUS LINK WITH ALICE SPRINGS
The Federal Court has been told Aboriginal people from Alice Springs maintained their ties with their traditional country, even when they were banned by law from the town.
A group of Arrernte Aboriginal people has lodged a native title claim over 166 parcels of Crown land within the Alice Springs town boundaries.
To succeed, the group must show the Federal Court it has an unbroken cultural connection with the land claimed.
Traditional owner Rosie Furber told the court even though Aboriginal people were legally barred from the Alice between 1928 and 1964, they still hunted and gathered foods in the area. - - - -
THE LATEST ON GERRY ADAM'S BID TO ENTER AUSTRALIA
Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams has won a skirmish in his battle to be allowed into Australia, with yesterday's Federal Court decision.
Mr Adams' application for a temporary business visa to enter Australia to publicise his autobiography was overruled by Immigration minister Philip Ruddock last year.
Mr Ruddock ruled that because of Mr Adams' association with the provisional I-R-A, he was of bad character and not fit to hold an Australian visa.
Justice Doug Drummond has now ruled that Mr Adams is allowed access to the documents Mr Philip Ruddock used to make his decision.
The ruling means Mr Ruddock must now release the information he used to reach his decision.
Lawyers for Mr Adams say they will look at the documents before taking the next step in the appeal process.
Legal spokesman, Sean Whelan, says Australia may be under pressure from Britain to prevent the Sinn Fein President visiting Australia.

Mr Whelan says it appears parties such as ASIO and the Irish embassy supported Mr Adams' visa application, but it was struck down by the Immigration Minister, who has gone to great lengths to prevent the planned visit.
Meanwhile, Sinn Fein Executive Committee member Dodie McGuiness says she's heartened by the ruling.
TELSTRA ACCUSED OF DRAGGING FEET ON COMPETITIVE REFORM
One of Australia's new telecommunications carriers, AAPT, has accused Telstra of dragging its feet on competitive reform.
AAPT's Chief Executive Officer, Larry Williams, says Telstra is frustrating competition by failing to provide AAPT with non-code dialing access as quickly as it could.
Non-code dialing access means customers don't need to dial in an access code to make long distance phone calls.
Mr Williams says AAPT has provided Telstra with 200,000 customer line numbers but Telstra is saying it can only transfer 12,500 to non-code access each week.
Mr Williams says he believes Telstra is capable of transferring 50,000 a week and its tardiness is having a significant impact on competition.
